books.title: Fahrenheit 451
books.author: Ray Bradbury
books.synopsis: In a society where firemen burn books instead of putting out fires, fireman Guy Montag starts to wonder what is inside them.

questions.prompt: What effect does Clarisse's question "Are you happy?" have on Montag?
options: It makes him laugh because it seems like a childish question
It convinces him to report her to the fire department
It confirms that his job gives his life meaning
It forces him to admit that his life is empty, even if he denies it
questions.explanation: The question unsettles Montag: when he thinks about it, he finds he is not happy and that his life with Mildred is empty.

questions.prompt: Why is the woman who chooses to burn with her books so important to Montag?
options: Because she proves to him that books are dangerous
Because she was an old friend of Mildred's
Because she makes him think there must be something valuable in books if someone would rather die with them
Because Beatty uses her as an example to promote him
questions.explanation: Montag concludes that there must be something in books, things we can't imagine, to make a woman stay in a burning house.

questions.prompt: According to Captain Beatty's explanation, how did book burning come about?
options: The government suddenly banned them after a war
People slowly gave them up: content got shorter, simpler and inoffensive to everyone, until censorship felt natural
Writers stopped publishing for lack of money
An accidental fire destroyed every library
questions.explanation: Beatty describes a gradual process: mass media, speed and the wish not to offend any minority made society reject books before they were ever banned.

questions.prompt: What does Montag's childhood memory of trying to fill a sieve with sand stand for?
options: His frustration when reading: he feels the words slip away and he can't hold on to them
The pointless work of the firemen
His wish to go back to childhood
questions.explanation: On the subway, Montag tries to memorize the Bible while an ad blares; the words run out like sand through the sieve.

questions.prompt: According to Faber, what three things is society missing?
options: Freedom of the press, elections and courts
More firemen, more TVs and more radios
Quality (texture) of information, leisure to digest it, and the right to act on what we learn
questions.explanation: Faber explains that what matters is not books as objects, but the quality of information, the time to digest it, and the freedom to act on it.

questions.prompt: What happens when Montag reads the poem "Dover Beach" to Mildred's friends?
options: They all applaud and ask him for more books
No one listens because the parlor walls are on
One of them cries, moved, and the others react with discomfort and rejection
Beatty walks in at that moment and arrests him
questions.explanation: Mrs. Phelps bursts into tears and Mrs. Bowles is outraged; the poem exposes the emotional emptiness they all try to ignore.

questions.prompt: What does Montag discover when the alarm takes the firemen to his own house?
options: That Faber had turned him in
questions.explanation: Mildred walks out of the house with a suitcase; she was the one who turned in the alarm.

questions.prompt: How do Granger and his group of drifters preserve books?
options: Each person memorizes a book or part of one to remember it and pass it on
They hide them in caves outside the city
They copy them by hand on loose sheets
They secretly send them to other countries
questions.explanation: Each of them "is" a book: they keep it in memory until the time comes to write the books down again.

questions.prompt: What is the meaning of the phoenix image Granger mentions at the end?
options: It is the symbol of the fire department
It announces that the war will never end
It is the name of the city they are heading to
Humanity destroys itself again and again, but it can rise from its ashes, this time remembering its mistakes
questions.explanation: After the city is bombed, Granger compares humanity to the phoenix; the difference is that people can remember what they did.

books.title: The Metamorphosis
books.author: Franz Kafka
books.synopsis: Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes up one morning changed into a monstrous insect, and his family must decide what to do with him.

questions.prompt: When he discovers his transformation, what worries Gregor first?
options: Finding a cure for his body
That his sister will be scared when she sees him
Having missed the train and being late for work
Escaping the house before they find him
questions.explanation: Before the horror of his new body, Gregor thinks about the train, his boss and the job he uses to support his family.

questions.prompt: Why does Gregor stay in a job he hates?
options: Because he dreams of becoming a director
Because his father owes the boss money and Gregor is paying it off
Because he doesn't know how to do anything else
Because his sister works at the same company
questions.explanation: Gregor puts up with the salesman job to pay off his parents' debt; he plans to quit as soon as it is paid.

questions.prompt: How does his father react when Gregor comes out of his room?
options: He forces him back with a cane and a newspaper, and Gregor gets hurt squeezing through the door
He hugs him and calls a doctor
He runs after the chief clerk to ask for help
questions.explanation: His father violently drives him back; Gregor is injured when he gets stuck in the doorframe.

questions.prompt: What role does Grete take on at the start of this part?
options: She refuses to go into Gregor's room
She looks for a doctor to cure him
She convinces her parents to move
She takes charge of feeding him and cleaning his room
questions.explanation: His sister is the only one who looks after him: she tests which foods he likes and cleans his room.

questions.prompt: Why does Gregor cling to the picture of the lady in furs when they empty his room?
options: Because he wants to hide behind it
Because there is food stuck to the picture
Because it is one of his last links to his human life and he doesn't want to lose it
Because he wants to scare his mother
questions.explanation: Seeing his furniture taken away, Gregor feels they are erasing his human past, and he protects the picture he framed himself.

questions.prompt: What does his father do at the end of Part II?
options: He locks him in and goes on a trip
He throws apples at him and one gets lodged in his back
He takes him to the hospital
questions.explanation: His father bombards Gregor with apples; one stays stuck in his back, and the wound stays with him until the end.

questions.prompt: What economic change happens in the Samsa family?
options: They all get jobs and also rent rooms to three lodgers
They sell the house and move to the country
questions.explanation: Without Gregor's salary, the father, the mother and Grete all work, and the family takes in three lodgers.

questions.prompt: What draws Gregor out of his room in front of the lodgers?
options: The light in the living room
questions.explanation: Moved by his sister's violin, Gregor crawls toward the living room and the lodgers see him.

questions.prompt: How does the family react after Gregor's death?
options: They fall into a deep depression
They decide to move in with the lodgers
They feel relief, take a trip to the country and make plans for Grete's future
They blame the cleaning woman and report her
questions.explanation: The family takes the day off, rides the tram to the country and thinks about finding Grete a husband: Gregor's death is a relief.

books.title: Animal Farm
books.author: George Orwell
books.synopsis: The animals on a farm drive out their human owner to govern themselves, but the new order does not turn out as they dreamed.

questions.prompt: What is the central message of Old Major's speech?
options: That the animals must work harder for Mr. Jones
That humans exploit animals and that they must rebel to be free
That pigs are superior to the rest
That the farm must be sold
questions.explanation: Major explains that man consumes without producing and lives off animal labor; only rebellion will free them.

questions.prompt: What role does the song "Beasts of England" play?
options: It is an anthem that unites the animals around the dream of rebellion
It is Mr. Jones's favorite song
It is used to call everyone to eat
questions.explanation: The song sums up the ideal of a future without humans and fills all the animals with enthusiasm.

questions.prompt: According to Major, how should animals treat one another?
options: Each species should look after only itself
All animals are comrades and none should copy the ways of man
questions.explanation: Major declares that all animals are equal and warns them not to take on human vices.

questions.prompt: What finally sets off the rebellion?
options: A plan carefully dated by the pigs
Jones and his men forget to feed the animals, who break into the store-shed hungry
questions.explanation: The rebellion is almost spontaneous: hunger drives the animals to attack when the humans neglect them.

questions.prompt: Why do the pigs take on the job of teaching and organizing?
options: Because they are considered the cleverest
Because the other animals voted for them
questions.explanation: Snowball, Napoleon and Squealer work out "Animalism" because they are recognized as the cleverest.

questions.prompt: What does the disappearance of the milk at the end of the chapter suggest?
options: That someone, presumably Napoleon, is already secretly taking advantage of common goods
That the cows stopped giving milk
That it was sold to buy seeds
questions.explanation: While the others bring in the harvest, the milk disappears: the first sign that the pigs will keep privileges for themselves.

questions.prompt: What does Boxer's motto, "I will work harder", reveal?
options: His ambition to lead the farm
That he plans to run away
His loyalty and blind faith in the cause, which make him easy to exploit
questions.explanation: Boxer answers every problem with more effort of his own, without questioning those in charge.

questions.prompt: Why are the Seven Commandments reduced to "Four legs good, two legs bad"?
options: To make fun of the hens
So that the less educated animals can remember them
To change the rules in favor of the dogs
questions.explanation: Snowball simplifies the commandments for those who cannot learn them; the sheep repeat it without thinking.

questions.prompt: How does Squealer justify the pigs keeping the milk and apples?
options: He says it is a reward for the harvest
He claims the pigs do brainwork that requires that food and that, if they fail, Jones will come back
He says the apples were rotten
He admits it is unfair but temporary
questions.explanation: Squealer uses the fear of Jones's return so that no one questions the privilege.

questions.prompt: Who leads the defense of the farm in the "Battle of the Cowshed"?
questions.explanation: Snowball, who had studied Julius Caesar's campaigns, plans the defense and is wounded.

questions.prompt: Why is Boxer upset after the battle?
options: Because he did not get a medal
Because he thinks he killed a stable lad and he does not want to take anyone's life
questions.explanation: Boxer feels remorse believing the boy is dead, though he was only stunned.

questions.prompt: What were Jones and his allies trying to do in this battle?
options: Take back the farm by force
questions.explanation: Jones, with men from the neighboring farms, tries to retake the property and is driven off.

questions.prompt: How does Napoleon get rid of Snowball?
options: He beats him in a vote
He chases him off the farm with the dogs he raised in secret
He sells him to a neighboring farmer
He convinces him to leave of his own free will
questions.explanation: In the middle of the debate about the windmill, nine huge dogs chase Snowball until he is off the farm.

questions.prompt: What does Napoleon decide about the Sunday meetings?
options: To abolish them: a committee of pigs will make the decisions
To open them to humans too
questions.explanation: The debates are gone; the animals will only receive orders.

questions.prompt: How does Squealer explain that Napoleon now supports the windmill he used to oppose?
options: He says Napoleon changed his mind after studying it
He claims the windmill was always Napoleon's idea and that opposing it was "tactics"
questions.explanation: Squealer rewrites history: Snowball's project becomes Napoleon's.

questions.prompt: What is misleading about the "voluntary" work on Sunday afternoons?
options: That it was never actually done
That any animal who skipped it had its rations cut by half
That only the pigs did it
questions.explanation: The work is "voluntary" in name only: refusing costs food.

questions.prompt: How is the commandment about beds changed when the pigs move into the farmhouse?
options: "With sheets" is added: no animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets
It is changed to "only pigs shall sleep in beds"
questions.explanation: The commandments are quietly rewritten to justify the pigs' privileges.

questions.prompt: Whom does Napoleon blame for the destruction of the windmill after the storm?
questions.explanation: Napoleon turns the absent Snowball into the enemy who gets the blame for any failure.

questions.prompt: Why do the hens rebel in this chapter?
options: Because they are not allowed to sleep
Because they want to move into the farmhouse
Because they are ordered to hand over their eggs to be sold
questions.explanation: Napoleon makes a deal to sell eggs; the hens resist and he crushes them by cutting off their food.

questions.prompt: What happens at the meeting where several animals "confess" to dealings with Snowball?
options: They are expelled from the farm
They are executed by the dogs
questions.explanation: The forced confessions end in executions: the violence becomes open.

questions.prompt: Why is singing "Beasts of England" banned?
options: Because the animals sang it badly
Because, according to the pigs, the rebellion is complete and the song no longer has a purpose
questions.explanation: The anthem of the shared dream is removed: it no longer suits the pigs for the animals to imagine a different society.

questions.prompt: What becomes of the commandment "No animal shall kill any other animal"?
questions.explanation: With two words added, the executions look legal.

questions.prompt: What happens in the timber deal with Frederick?
options: Frederick pays twice what was agreed
Pilkington ends up with the timber
Frederick pays with forged banknotes, then attacks the farm and blows up the windmill
questions.explanation: Napoleon is cheated and the farm suffers the Battle of the Windmill.

questions.prompt: What does the scene of Squealer fallen next to a ladder and a pot of paint reveal?
options: That he was painting the barn
That he was trying to escape
That the pigs change the commandments at night
questions.explanation: Soon after, the commandment about alcohol reads "to excess"; hardly anyone understands what they saw.

questions.prompt: What is Boxer's real fate?
options: He dies in a veterinary hospital
He is sold to a horse slaughterer
questions.explanation: Benjamin reads the sign on the van: it belongs to the horse slaughterer. Squealer denies it.

questions.prompt: How does the farm become a "Republic"?
options: Napoleon, the only candidate, is elected president unanimously
Through a rebellion of the sheep
questions.explanation: The democratic form hides absolute power.

questions.prompt: Why do the pigs tolerate the return of Moses the raven and his Sugarcandy Mountain?
options: Because the promise of a future paradise helps the animals bear their present misery
questions.explanation: The comforting story defuses the discontent of the hungry animals.

questions.prompt: What do the sheep now shout when the pigs walk on two legs?
questions.explanation: The slogan is turned upside down and no one protests.

questions.prompt: What do the Seven Commandments become?
options: A single commandment: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others"
They are restored as they were at the start
They are erased with nothing to replace them
questions.explanation: The phrase sums up the betrayal of the revolution.

questions.prompt: What does the final scene mean, when the animals can no longer tell the pigs from the men?
options: That the pigs have become identical to the oppressors they rebelled against
That the humans took back the farm
That all the animals made peace
questions.explanation: The cycle closes: the new elite repeats the exploitation of the old one.

books.title: The Little Prince
books.author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
books.synopsis: A pilot stranded in the Sahara Desert meets a little prince who comes from another planet.

questions.prompt: What did the grown-ups see in the narrator's Drawing Number One?
questions.explanation: It was a boa constrictor digesting an elephant, but the grown-ups only saw a hat.

questions.prompt: What is the narrator criticizing with this story?
options: That grown-ups lack imagination and need everything explained to them
questions.explanation: Discouraged by the grown-ups, he gives up drawing and becomes a pilot.

questions.prompt: What does the little prince ask the narrator when they meet?
questions.explanation: "If you please... draw me a sheep!"

questions.prompt: Why is the little prince happy with the drawing of a box?
options: Because he imagines the sheep inside, just as he wanted it
questions.explanation: The little prince sees what is inside: imagination completes the drawing.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator discover about where the little prince comes from?
options: That he is a pilot's son
That he lives in a nearby oasis
That he is lost from a caravan
That he comes from another planet
questions.explanation: Laughing at the plane that "fell from the sky", the little prince reveals that he comes from another planet.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator get information from the little prince?
options: Through direct questions the little prince answers
Little by little, from words dropped by chance, since the little prince never answers what he is asked
questions.explanation: The little prince asks a lot but hardly ever answers; the narrator pieces his story together.

questions.prompt: Why did no one believe the Turkish astronomer the first time he presented asteroid B-612?
questions.explanation: When he presented it again in European dress, everyone believed him.

questions.prompt: According to the narrator, what do grown-ups care about?
options: Figures: age, money, number of brothers
questions.explanation: Grown-ups ask about figures, not about what matters.

questions.prompt: Why must baobabs be pulled up while they are small?
options: Because the sheep don't eat them
Because if they grow, their roots can destroy the planet
questions.explanation: Neglecting a young baobab lets it take over and split the planet to pieces.

questions.prompt: What lesson is in the daily discipline with the baobabs?
options: That you have to move to another planet
That small problems must be dealt with in time, steadily
questions.explanation: "It is a question of discipline": taking care every day of what could turn into a disaster.

questions.prompt: How can the little prince see several sunsets in one day?
options: By moving his chair a few steps on his tiny planet
questions.explanation: His planet is so small that he only has to move his chair.

questions.prompt: What does the day he watched the sunset forty-three times reveal?
options: That he wanted to impress the narrator
questions.explanation: "One loves the sunset, when one is so sad."

questions.prompt: Why does the little prince get angry with the narrator?
options: Because he didn't draw him another sheep
Because the narrator left him alone
Because the narrator says he is busy with "matters of consequence" and doesn't care if the sheep eats his flower
questions.explanation: For the little prince, his one and only flower is what truly matters.

questions.prompt: What finally comforts the little prince in this chapter?
options: The narrator holds him and promises to draw protection for his flower
questions.explanation: The narrator drops his engine work and promises a muzzle for the sheep and armor for the flower.

questions.prompt: What is the little prince's flower like?
questions.explanation: She asks for a screen, a glass globe and care; she tells small lies so he will look after her.

questions.prompt: What does the little prince later admit about his relationship with the flower?
options: That he should have judged her by her deeds and not by her words
That it was better not to have a flower
That he was right to doubt her
questions.explanation: The flower filled his world with fragrance and light; he was too young to know how to love her.

questions.prompt: What does the flower tell the little prince before he leaves?
options: To take the volcanoes with him
That she loves him and has been silly, and that she doesn't need the glass globe
questions.explanation: The flower asks his forgiveness and wishes him happiness.

questions.prompt: What does the flower mean by "I must endure the presence of two or three caterpillars if I wish to become acquainted with the butterflies"?
options: That the little prince is a caterpillar
That you have to accept some discomforts to get something beautiful
questions.explanation: Beauty has a cost; the flower accepts the trouble.

questions.prompt: Why does the king only give orders that can be obeyed?
options: Because authority must be based on reason
questions.explanation: "One must require from each one the duty which each one can perform."

questions.prompt: According to the king, what is the hardest thing?
questions.explanation: "It is much more difficult to judge oneself than to judge others."

questions.prompt: What does the conceited man want from others?
questions.explanation: For the conceited man, everyone else is an admirer.

questions.prompt: What trait shows that the conceited man only listens to praise?
options: He only talks about his planet
He hears nothing that is not praise
questions.explanation: Conceited people never hear anything but praise.

questions.prompt: Why does the tippler drink?
options: To forget that he is ashamed of drinking
questions.explanation: A vicious circle that leaves the little prince puzzled.

questions.prompt: What feeling does this visit leave the little prince with?
questions.explanation: He leaves puzzled and sad: "The grown-ups are certainly very, very odd."

questions.prompt: What does the businessman do with the stars?
options: He counts them and claims to own them so he can be rich
questions.explanation: He writes their number on a paper and puts it in a bank.

questions.prompt: Why does the little prince think his way of owning things is different?
options: Because he is useful to what he owns: he waters his flower and cleans out his volcanoes
questions.explanation: For him, owning means taking care.

questions.prompt: Why does the lamplighter never rest anymore?
options: Because his planet turns faster and faster and his orders have not changed
questions.explanation: Now the planet turns once a minute and he still follows orders.

questions.prompt: Why is the lamplighter the only one who doesn't seem ridiculous to the little prince?
options: Because he cares about something other than himself
questions.explanation: His work has meaning because he looks beyond himself.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the geographer record flowers?
options: Because they are ephemeral and he only records what is eternal
questions.explanation: Geography books only record things that do not change.

questions.prompt: What does the little prince feel when he learns his flower is ephemeral?
options: Regret at having left her alone
questions.explanation: It is his first moment of regret.

questions.prompt: Which planet does the little prince visit on the geographer's advice?
questions.explanation: The geographer recommends the Earth, which "has a good reputation".

questions.prompt: In what tone does the narrator describe the Earth, with its kings, geographers and lamplighters?
options: Ironically, as a planet full of grown-ups like the ones already seen
questions.explanation: The Earth multiplies the characters the little prince has already met.

questions.prompt: What does the snake offer the little prince?
options: To help him return to his planet someday
questions.explanation: Whomever it touches, it "sends back to the earth from whence he came".

questions.prompt: Faced with the loneliness of the desert, what does the snake answer?
options: That the desert is full of people
That it is also lonely among men
That he should look for a king
questions.explanation: Loneliness does not depend on how many people there are.

questions.prompt: According to the desert flower, why do men go from place to place?
options: Because they have no roots and the wind blows them away
Because they are looking for water
questions.explanation: The flower has only seen one caravan: men have no roots.

questions.prompt: How many men does the flower think exist?
questions.explanation: Her limited view shows how little she knows of the world.

questions.prompt: What does the little prince hear when he speaks from the mountain?
options: Only the echo of his own words
questions.explanation: The echo repeats everything he says.

questions.prompt: What does the little prince conclude about men from the echo?
options: That they don't know how to talk
That they have no imagination and repeat whatever is said to them
questions.explanation: He remembers that his flower always spoke first.

questions.prompt: Why does the little prince cry when he finds the rose garden?
options: Because he discovers thousands of flowers just like his, which he thought was unique
questions.explanation: He feels less rich: he thought he had a flower that was unique in the universe.

questions.prompt: How many roses were in the garden?
questions.explanation: Five thousand roses, all just like his.

questions.prompt: According to the fox, what does "tame" mean?
questions.explanation: When they tame each other, two beings become unique to each other.

questions.prompt: What secret does the fox tell the little prince?
options: How to get back to his planet
That what is essential is invisible to the eye, and one can only see rightly with the heart
questions.explanation: And that the time he spent on his rose is what makes her so important.

questions.prompt: According to the railway switchman, what are the train passengers looking for?
options: No one knows, not even they do
questions.explanation: They travel without knowing what they are after, and they are never happy where they are.

questions.prompt: Who looks out the window, according to the switchman?
questions.explanation: Only the children know what they are looking for.

questions.prompt: What does the merchant sell?
questions.explanation: Pills that save fifty-three minutes a week.

questions.prompt: What would the little prince do with those fifty-three minutes?
options: Walk slowly toward a spring of fresh water
questions.explanation: He values the experience, not the shortcut.

questions.prompt: What situation is the narrator in during this chapter?
options: He runs out of water and they set off to look for a well
questions.explanation: It is the eighth day since his breakdown and they drink the last drop.

questions.prompt: According to the little prince, what makes the desert beautiful?
options: That somewhere it hides a well
questions.explanation: What is invisible gives value to what is visible.

questions.prompt: Why is the water from the well special?
options: Because it is the only water in the world
Because it was born of the walk, the song of the pulley and shared effort, and it is good for the heart
questions.explanation: It is like a present.

questions.prompt: What does the little prince remember in this chapter?
options: That the anniversary of his arrival on Earth is coming
questions.explanation: Tomorrow it will be one year since he fell near this place.

questions.prompt: What gift does the little prince leave the narrator?
options: Stars that laugh: when he looks at the sky, he will know the little prince is laughing on one of them
questions.explanation: Every star will be like a little bell for him.

questions.prompt: How does the little prince leave the Earth?
options: The snake bites him and he falls gently onto the sand
questions.explanation: He falls "as gently as a tree falls", without a sound.

questions.prompt: What did the narrator forget when he drew the muzzle?
questions.explanation: That is why he wonders whether the sheep has eaten the flower.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator ask the reader at the end?
options: That if they meet a child with golden hair, they write to him right away
questions.explanation: The story stays open and tied to hope.

books.title: Chronicle of a Death Foretold
books.author: Gabriel García Márquez
books.synopsis: Twenty-seven years later, a narrator pieces together the day Santiago Nasar was murdered, a crime the whole town knew was going to happen.

questions.prompt: What device does the novel use from the very first line?
options: It hides the ending until the last page
It announces right away that Santiago Nasar will be murdered
It opens with the killer's dream
It is told from the point of view of the dead victim
questions.explanation: The interest is not in what will happen, but in how it happened and why no one stopped it.

questions.prompt: Why is the town stirred up that morning?
options: Because the bishop is arriving by boat
questions.explanation: Santiago gets up early to greet the bishop.

questions.prompt: Who tells the story?
options: A friend of Santiago's who pieces the events together years later
questions.explanation: He gathers testimonies like a journalistic investigation.

questions.prompt: What is Bayardo San Román like when he arrives in town?
options: An old friend of the Vicarios
questions.explanation: He dazzles everyone and decides to marry Ángela.

questions.prompt: Why does Ángela agree to marry Bayardo?
options: Because she falls in love right away
Because of pressure from her family, who see him as a great match
questions.explanation: She says she does not love him, but her family insists.

questions.prompt: What happens on the wedding night?
options: Bayardo returns Ángela to her family because he discovers she was not a virgin
questions.explanation: That event sets off the crime.

questions.prompt: What do the Vicario twins do before the crime?
options: They tell a great many people that they are going to kill Santiago
questions.explanation: It seems they want someone to stop them.

questions.prompt: Why does almost no one step in to prevent the crime?
options: Out of fear of the twins
Because of a mix of disbelief, assuming someone else would warn him, and acceptance of the code of honor
questions.explanation: Collective responsibility is the central theme.

questions.prompt: What does the mayor do when he finds out?
options: He takes their knives away and thinks the matter is settled
questions.explanation: But the twins get other knives.

questions.prompt: What does the autopsy done by Father Carmen Amador reveal?
options: A clumsy, brutal procedure done by an untrained priest
That Santiago died of another cause
That there was a third guilty party
questions.explanation: It shows how poorly equipped the town is.

questions.prompt: What does Ángela Vicario do for years after the crime?
questions.explanation: She writes hundreds of letters that get no answer.

questions.prompt: What happens when Bayardo comes back?
options: He arrives with all the letters, unopened
questions.explanation: The ending raises questions about love and honor.

questions.prompt: Why does Plácida Linero close the front door?
options: Because she thinks Santiago is already inside and that the twins are about to come in
questions.explanation: One of the tragic coincidences that seal his fate.

questions.prompt: What is the point of the pile-up of coincidences at the end?
options: That fate and collective inaction combined so that no one prevented it
That the crime was unavoidable for everyone
questions.explanation: The chronicle shows how a whole town let it happen.

questions.prompt: What is left unresolved at the end?
options: Whether Santiago was really the one who dishonored Ángela
questions.explanation: The doubt makes the crime even more absurd.

books.title: Aura
books.author: Carlos Fuentes
books.synopsis: A young historian takes a job in an old house in downtown Mexico City and meets an elderly widow and her niece Aura.

questions.prompt: What is special about the narrative voice in Aura?
options: It is in the first person
It is an omniscient third-person narrator
It is in the second person: "you"
questions.explanation: The reader becomes Felipe Montero.

questions.prompt: Why does Felipe Montero feel the newspaper ad is meant for him?
options: Because it has his name on it
Because it describes his profile exactly: a young historian who knows French
Because it was mailed to him
Because he was looking for a house
questions.explanation: All that is missing is his name.

questions.prompt: What job does Señora Consuelo offer him?
options: To edit and finish the memoirs of her late husband, General Llorente
questions.explanation: On the condition that he live in the house.

questions.prompt: What is the house on Donceles Street like?
options: Dark, damp and cut off from the world
questions.explanation: A space outside of time.

questions.prompt: What strikes Felipe about Aura?
options: Her green eyes and her presence, which seems to depend on the old woman
questions.explanation: Felipe feels drawn to her.

questions.prompt: What does the old woman do in her bedroom?
options: She prays before religious images, in a room full of votive candles
questions.explanation: An atmosphere of worship and devotion.

questions.prompt: What does Felipe discover when he reads the general's papers?
options: Details of Consuelo's youth and her life with the general
questions.explanation: The story of the past starts to be reflected in the present.

questions.prompt: What disturbing scene does Felipe witness in the kitchen?
options: Aura cutting the throat of a goat while the old woman copies her gestures in her room
questions.explanation: It suggests a supernatural bond.

questions.prompt: What does the matching of gestures between Aura and the old woman suggest?
options: That they are linked in a mysterious way, almost as if they were the same person
questions.explanation: It is one of the keys to the fantastic element.

questions.prompt: What change does Felipe notice in Aura?
options: That she seems to have aged
That she has changed her name
questions.explanation: Her age seems to change.

questions.prompt: What does Aura ask of Felipe?
options: To talk to the old woman
questions.explanation: The promise of eternal love is central.

questions.prompt: What atmosphere dominates this part?
questions.explanation: Reality dissolves.

questions.prompt: What do the photographs of the general and Consuelo reveal?
options: That the general looks like Felipe and the young Consuelo looks like Aura
questions.explanation: The final revelation.

questions.prompt: What was the young Consuelo trying to do, according to the papers?
options: Keep or regain her youth with plants and potions
questions.explanation: The wish to stop time explains Aura.

questions.prompt: What does Felipe understand at the end?
options: That Aura and Consuelo are the same woman
questions.explanation: The ending brings past and present together.

books.title: Lazarillo de Tormes
books.author: Anonymous
books.synopsis: Lázaro, a poor boy from Salamanca, tells in the first person how he survived by serving different masters in 16th-century Spain.

questions.prompt: Whom is Lázaro addressing when he tells his life story?
options: "Your Worship", who has asked him to tell his case
questions.explanation: The book is a long letter to "Your Worship", who asked Lázaro to tell "the case" in full.

questions.prompt: What contrast does the prologue draw between nobles and those who, like Lázaro, started with nothing?
options: That nobles deserve their fortune because of their lineage
That those who get ahead by "rowing" with strength and skill deserve more credit than those who inherit their rank
That poverty is a punishment from God
That no one can change their social position
questions.explanation: Lázaro ironically defends the merit of those who prosper through their own effort over those who inherit "noble estates".

questions.prompt: What lesson does the blind man teach Lázaro by slamming his head against the stone bull in Salamanca?
options: That he must respect sacred images
That he must never lie to his master
That a blind man's boy must know more than the devil
That stone is harder than need
questions.explanation: After the blow, the blind man tells him that a blind man's boy "must know one point more than the devil": Lázaro wakes up to cunning.

questions.prompt: In the grapes episode, how does the blind man find out that Lázaro cheated him?
options: Because he counted the grapes left on the bunch
Because he was eating two at a time and Lázaro said nothing, so he figured the boy was eating three at a time
questions.explanation: The blind man breaks their deal to eat them one by one; since Lázaro doesn't complain, he deduces that the boy was cheating him too.

questions.prompt: How does Lázaro finally get revenge on the blind man before leaving him?
options: He makes him jump into a stone post, pretending there is a stream
He leaves him in the middle of the countryside at night
He steals all the money from his purse
He reports him to the law in Escalona
questions.explanation: In Escalona, Lázaro places the blind man in front of a post and tells him to jump over the water; the blind man hits the post and Lázaro runs off.

chapters.title: Second treatise: the priest of Maqueda

questions.prompt: Compared with the blind man, what is the priest of Maqueda like?
options: Even stingier: Lázaro goes hungrier with him
questions.explanation: Lázaro says he escaped the thunder only to run into the lightning: the priest is even meaner than the blind man.

questions.prompt: How does Lázaro get to the bread kept in the chest?
options: He breaks the lock with a stone
He asks the priest's maid for it
He buys a key from a tinker who comes by the house
He gets in through a cellar window
questions.explanation: A tinker sells him a key to the chest; then Lázaro pretends that mice (and a "snake") are to blame.

questions.prompt: How does the priest discover the trick?
options: He finds crumbs in the boy's bed
A neighbor sees Lázaro open the chest
The key, which Lázaro keeps in his mouth while he sleeps, whistles and the priest thinks it is the snake
questions.explanation: When he strikes the supposed snake in the straw, the priest finds the key in Lázaro's mouth and throws him out.

questions.prompt: What paradox defines the squire of Toledo?
options: He looks rich and honorable, but he is so poor that Lázaro has to beg to feed him
He is rich but lives like a beggar out of greed
He is noble and generous with the poor
He is a thief dressed as a gentleman
questions.explanation: The squire cares about appearances (he even pretends to have eaten by picking his teeth), while Lázaro supports him with alms.

questions.prompt: What new feeling does Lázaro have toward this master, unlike the earlier ones?
options: Hatred and a desire for revenge
Pity: he feels sorry for him and shares what he gets
questions.explanation: Lázaro says that, unlike the others, he felt pity for this one, and he feeds him even though he is his master.

questions.prompt: Why does the squire disappear at the end of the treatise?
options: He inherits a fortune in Old Castile
He runs away to avoid paying the rent on the house and the bed to those who come to collect
He is arrested for a duel
questions.explanation: When they come to collect, the squire goes out "to change a coin" and never comes back, leaving Lázaro alone with the creditors.

chapters.title: Fourth treatise: the friar of the Order of Mercy

questions.prompt: What trait of the friar of the Order of Mercy does Lázaro point out?
options: That he was extremely stingy with bread
That he was a great walker, fonder of the streets than of the choir
questions.explanation: The friar spent his life walking from place to place; Lázaro couldn't keep up with "his trotting" and left him.

questions.prompt: What did the friar give Lázaro?
questions.explanation: The friar gave him the first shoes he ever wore out, though they didn't last long because of all the walking.

questions.prompt: What does the pardoner do for a living?
options: He sells papal bulls (indulgences), using tricks to win people over
He sells water around the city
He collects taxes for the king
questions.explanation: The pardoner preaches and sells bulls, and turns to deceit when people don't want to buy them.

questions.prompt: What trick does the pardoner stage with the constable?
options: The constable arrests anyone who doesn't buy bulls
They forge letters from the Pope
They fake a quarrel and a "miracle": the constable falls down as if possessed and the pardoner "heals" him
They hide the bulls so the price goes up
questions.explanation: After the fake miracle, the impressed townspeople buy bulls in droves; Lázaro realizes it was all set up.

questions.prompt: What does Lázaro learn as a witness to this master?
options: That it pays to become a friar
That deceit can be dressed up as religion for profit
questions.explanation: The treatise satirizes corruption in the sale of bulls: people's faith is exploited with theater.

questions.prompt: What job does the chaplain give Lázaro?
options: Water seller: selling water around Toledo with a donkey
questions.explanation: Lázaro works as a water seller; it is his first "good" job where he keeps some earnings.

questions.prompt: What does Lázaro do with what he saves in four years?
options: He buys secondhand clothes and a sword to look like a gentleman, and quits the job
He gives it to the church
questions.explanation: Now "very respectably dressed", Lázaro gives up the donkey: like the squire, he cares about the appearance of honor.

chapters.title: Seventh treatise: the archpriest of San Salvador

questions.prompt: What "royal office" does Lázaro get in the end?
questions.explanation: As town crier he advertises wines and walks with condemned criminals; he sees it as a safe and profitable job.

questions.prompt: Whom does Lázaro marry, in a match arranged by the archpriest of San Salvador?
options: The daughter of a rich merchant
questions.explanation: The archpriest marries him to his maid and gives them a house and help.

questions.prompt: How does Lázaro respond to the rumors about his wife and the archpriest?
options: He chooses to ignore them to keep his comfortable life, and says he is at the height of his good fortune
He confronts the archpriest in public
He reports the matter to the Inquisition
questions.explanation: The ending is ironic: Lázaro's "honor" depends on accepting a dishonorable situation in exchange for comfort.

books.title: Hamlet
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.synopsis: The Prince of Denmark receives a revelation that forces him to choose between doubt and action, in a court where no one says what they think.

questions.prompt: What does the ghost reveal to Hamlet?
options: That he died in battle against Norway
That Claudius murdered him by pouring poison in his ear while he slept
That Polonius plotted to kill him
questions.explanation: The ghost of the king says his brother Claudius poisoned him to take the crown and the queen, and asks for revenge.

questions.prompt: What bothers Hamlet about his mother, Gertrude, from the start?
options: That she wants to send him to England
That she married Claudius very soon after his father's death
questions.explanation: Hamlet laments the hasty wedding: "the funeral baked meats did coldly furnish forth the marriage tables".

questions.prompt: What does Hamlet tell Horatio and Marcellus after seeing the ghost?
options: That he will kill Claudius that very night
That he will flee to Wittenberg
That he will give up the throne to Laertes
That he may put on a strange or mad manner, and he makes them swear to keep silent
questions.explanation: Hamlet warns that he might take on an "antic disposition" and asks them not to reveal what they saw.

questions.prompt: How does Polonius explain Hamlet's strange behavior?
options: As madness from love for Ophelia, because she rejected him on his advice
As the effect of a poison
questions.explanation: Polonius believes Ophelia's rejection drove Hamlet out of his mind, and he tells the king and queen.

questions.prompt: Why does Claudius send for Rosencrantz and Guildenstern?
options: To take a message to Norway
To spy on Hamlet and find out the cause of his change
questions.explanation: They are Hamlet's old schoolfellows, used by the king and queen to draw him out; Hamlet soon sees through it.

questions.prompt: What plan does Hamlet come up with when the players arrive?
options: To use the players to escape the castle
To ask the players to kill Claudius
To stage a play like his father's murder to watch Claudius's reaction
To write a play to win Ophelia's love
questions.explanation: "The play's the thing wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king": Hamlet wants to confirm what the ghost told him.

questions.prompt: What does Claudius's reaction during the play confirm?
options: His innocence: he applauds the play
His guilt: he rises in distress and stops the performance
questions.explanation: On seeing the poisoning scene, Claudius calls for lights and leaves: Hamlet no longer doubts the ghost.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't Hamlet kill Claudius when he finds him praying?
options: Because he fears that, killed while praying, his soul would go to heaven
Because he decides to forgive him
questions.explanation: Hamlet wants to kill him in sin; ironically, Claudius admits he cannot truly pray.

questions.prompt: What happens in the queen's chamber?
options: Hamlet kills Polonius, who was spying hidden behind a curtain
Ophelia declares her love for Hamlet
questions.explanation: Thinking it is the king, Hamlet runs his sword through the curtain and kills Polonius; the ghost appears again.

questions.prompt: What does Claudius intend by sending Hamlet to England?
options: For him to sign a peace treaty
For him to be executed there, through sealed letters
For him to marry an English princess
questions.explanation: The letters carried by Rosencrantz and Guildenstern order Hamlet's death.

questions.prompt: What trap do Claudius and Laertes plan against Hamlet?
options: A duel with an unblunted, poisoned sword, and a poisoned cup as backup
questions.explanation: Laertes wants to avenge his father and Claudius makes sure of the outcome with double poison.

questions.prompt: What happens to Ophelia in this act?
options: She goes mad after her father's death and drowns in a brook
She flees to France with Laertes
questions.explanation: Ophelia hands out flowers while singing songs; Gertrude later describes her death in the water.

questions.prompt: What thought does Yorick's skull prompt in Hamlet?
options: That he should give up revenge
That death makes everyone equal and the body returns to dust, whether jester or king
questions.explanation: Before the skull of the jester he knew as a child, Hamlet reflects on how brief life is (even Alexander the Great ends up as dust).

questions.prompt: How does Gertrude die?
options: Laertes wounds her in the duel
She takes her own life when she learns the truth
She drinks by mistake from the poisoned cup meant for Hamlet
questions.explanation: She drinks to Hamlet from the cup Claudius had poisoned; before dying, she warns of the poison.

questions.prompt: What does Hamlet ask of Horatio before he dies?
options: To bury him next to Ophelia
To take the throne of Denmark
To go on living to tell his story truthfully
questions.explanation: Hamlet stops him from drinking the poison and charges him with telling what happened. His last words: "The rest is silence".

books.title: The House of Bernarda Alba
books.author: Federico García Lorca
books.synopsis: After her second husband dies, Bernarda shuts her five daughters away in strict mourning, while desire and rivalry grow behind the walls.

questions.prompt: What does Bernarda impose on her daughters after the funeral?
options: Eight years of mourning shut indoors, without even "the wind from the street" getting in
questions.explanation: Bernarda orders strict mourning that turns the house into a prison.

questions.prompt: Why does Pepe el Romano want to marry Angustias?
options: Because she is the youngest and prettiest
Because she is the richest heiress, thanks to her father's inheritance
Because she is the only unmarried one
questions.explanation: Angustias, the daughter of the first husband and almost forty, has her own fortune, and that draws Pepe.

questions.prompt: What does Adela's gesture with her green dress reveal?
options: Her plan to become a nun
Her wish to live and her rebellion against mourning
questions.explanation: Adela puts on the green dress she meant to wear for the first time: the color clashes with the black of mourning and signals her rebellion.

questions.prompt: What mismatch raises suspicion about Pepe's visits?
options: Bernarda saw him come in through the yard
Angustias says he left at half past one, but others heard him leave around four
questions.explanation: The times don't match: after talking with Angustias, Pepe stays with another sister, Adela.

questions.prompt: Where does the stolen picture of Pepe that belonged to Angustias turn up?
questions.explanation: Martirio says it was a joke; the theft shows that she is also in love with Pepe.

questions.prompt: Why is Adela so distressed when Librada's daughter is lynched?
options: Because she was her best friend
Because the woman is punished for having a child outside marriage, which Adela fears for herself
Because Librada works in the house
Because Pepe takes part in the lynching
questions.explanation: While Bernarda calls for her death, Adela holds her belly: the village punishes what she is living in secret.

questions.prompt: What does Bernarda do when she finds Adela with Pepe?
options: She throws Adela out of the house
She forces Pepe to marry Adela
She grabs the shotgun and goes out to shoot at Pepe
questions.explanation: Bernarda fires; Martirio, out of jealousy, says Pepe is dead, though he actually ran away.

questions.prompt: What does Adela do when she believes Pepe is dead?
options: She runs off to the village
She asks her mother for forgiveness
She locks herself in and hangs herself
questions.explanation: Martirio's lie causes the final tragedy.

questions.prompt: What does Bernarda's final reaction to Adela's death reveal?
options: That she cares more about appearances and honor than about grief: she orders people to say Adela died a virgin and demands silence
That she blames Martirio in public
That she decides to end the mourning
questions.explanation: "My daughter has died a virgin!... Silence!": public honor above everything.

books.author: George Orwell
books.synopsis: In a State that watches every move and rewrites the past, a Party official begins to have secret doubts.

questions.prompt: What is Winston's job at the Ministry of Truth?
options: Rewriting old documents and newspapers so they match what the Party says
questions.explanation: Winston alters the historical record: the past is made to fit the official version of the present.

questions.prompt: Why is it dangerous for Winston to keep a diary?
options: Because writing is banned for everyone
Because thinking and recording your own ideas is thoughtcrime
Because his boss is watching him
questions.explanation: In the diary he writes "DOWN WITH BIG BROTHER": a private act the State punishes.

questions.prompt: According to Syme, what is the goal of Newspeak?
options: To make learning easier for children
To shrink the vocabulary so that certain ideas become impossible to think
questions.explanation: If there are no words for dissent, dissenting thought becomes impossible.

questions.prompt: What does the room above Mr. Charrington's shop mean to Winston?
options: A private refuge where he and Julia feel free
questions.explanation: With no telescreen in sight, the room seems to be a space outside the Party's control.

questions.prompt: What happens in the middle of a speech during Hate Week?
options: The official enemy changes and everyone acts as if it had always been that way
A bomb goes off in the square
questions.explanation: The war switches from Eurasia to Eastasia mid-sentence: doublethink in action.

questions.prompt: How does Part Two end?
options: Winston and Julia are arrested: there was a hidden telescreen and Charrington was in the Thought Police
questions.explanation: The refuge was a trap: "You are the dead", says the voice behind the picture.

questions.prompt: What does O'Brien want when he tortures Winston?
options: To get the names of other rebels
To use him as a spy
Not just his obedience, but for him to truly believe whatever the Party says, like 2 + 2 = 5
questions.explanation: The Party wants to control the mind: Winston must see five fingers if he is told to.

questions.prompt: What is in Room 101?
options: The worst thing in the world for each prisoner; for Winston, rats
questions.explanation: Faced with the rats, Winston betrays Julia and begs them to do it to her.

questions.prompt: How does Winston end up?
options: Released but defeated: he loves Big Brother
questions.explanation: The last sentence marks total defeat: the Party has conquered even his feelings.

books.title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
books.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
books.synopsis: A London lawyer looks into the strange bond between his respectable friend, Dr. Jekyll, and a repulsive man named Hyde.

questions.prompt: What does Enfield tell about Hyde?
options: That he ran into a little girl and trampled her calmly
That he set a house on fire
questions.explanation: Hyde's cold cruelty horrifies every witness from the first scene.

questions.prompt: What is puzzling about how Hyde pays the girl's family?
options: He pays twice what was asked
He covers it with a check signed by a highly respected man
questions.explanation: Hyde goes through a door and comes back with a check from an honorable man: Utterson guesses who it is.

questions.prompt: What do Utterson and Enfield agree on at the end of their talk?
options: Never to speak of the matter again
To go to the police together
To watch the door every night
questions.explanation: Both prefer to stay silent: the discretion of Victorian gentlemen protects the secret.

questions.prompt: What does Jekyll's will say?
options: That if he dies or disappears, everything goes to Edward Hyde
That he leaves his fortune to a hospital
That Lanyon will be his heir
questions.explanation: The "disappearance" clause makes Utterson fear that Hyde is blackmailing Jekyll.

questions.prompt: What impression does Hyde make on Utterson when he finally meets him?
options: That he is an elegant, kind man
That he is a sick old man
A disgust he can't explain, with no clear deformity to account for it
That he looks a lot like Jekyll
questions.explanation: No one can describe what is wrong with Hyde, but everyone feels disgust: they sense something evil in him.

questions.prompt: What does Dr. Lanyon think of Jekyll?
options: That he is the best doctor in London
That they grew apart because Jekyll's scientific ideas became fanciful
questions.explanation: Lanyon calls Jekyll's theories unscientific nonsense.

chapters.title: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease

questions.prompt: How does Jekyll respond when Utterson brings up the will?
options: He tells him not to worry and, if anything happens to him, to make sure Hyde gets his rights
He changes the will right away
He admits Hyde is blackmailing him
He gets angry and throws him out
questions.explanation: Jekyll insists he can be rid of Hyde whenever he wants, and asks Utterson to protect him.

questions.prompt: What does Jekyll's attitude in this scene suggest?
options: That he has a link to Hyde he would rather hide
That he plans to flee London
questions.explanation: His apparent calm contrasts with the mystery he is protecting.

questions.prompt: Who witnesses the murder of Sir Danvers Carew?
options: A maid looking out of the window
questions.explanation: The maid sees Hyde furiously beat a kind old man with a cane.

questions.prompt: What clue links the crime to Jekyll?
options: The broken cane, which Utterson had given to Jekyll
questions.explanation: Utterson recognizes the weapon and leads the police to Hyde's house in Soho.

questions.prompt: What do they find at Hyde's house?
options: Half of the cane and a burned checkbook, but Hyde has vanished
questions.explanation: Hyde disappears: no one has a photograph of him and few can describe him.

questions.prompt: What does Jekyll assure Utterson after the crime?
options: That he is done with Hyde forever
That he will turn Hyde in
questions.explanation: Jekyll shows a letter from Hyde saying he has fled.

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Guest find when he compares the handwriting?
options: That the letter is from Lanyon
That Hyde's letter and a note from Jekyll are in the same hand, only sloped differently
That it is a woman's handwriting
questions.explanation: Utterson concludes, horrified, that Jekyll forged the letter to cover for a murderer.

questions.prompt: What wrong conclusion does Utterson draw?
options: That Jekyll forges documents to protect Hyde
questions.explanation: Utterson still can't imagine the truth: that Jekyll and Hyde are the same person.

questions.prompt: What happens to Lanyon shortly after a dinner with Jekyll?
options: He falls ill after a great shock and dies within a few weeks
questions.explanation: Lanyon says he has had a shock he will never recover from, and he won't hear Jekyll's name.

questions.prompt: What does Lanyon leave for Utterson?
options: An envelope to be opened only if Jekyll dies or disappears
questions.explanation: The envelope's condition strangely echoes the one in Jekyll's will.

questions.prompt: How does Jekyll's behavior change in this chapter?
options: He marries and gives up science
He turns himself in to the police
After a period of social life, he shuts himself away again and refuses visitors
questions.explanation: Jekyll's isolation signals that something serious is happening.

questions.prompt: What do Utterson and Enfield see at Jekyll's window?
options: A look of utter terror that makes him slam the window shut
questions.explanation: Jekyll is talking with them until something terrible changes him before their eyes.

questions.prompt: What effect does the scene have on the two friends?
options: They walk away in silence, horrified by what they saw
They go into the house to help him
questions.explanation: The scene hints at the transformation without explaining it.

questions.prompt: Why does Poole come to Utterson?
options: He thinks his master has been murdered and someone else is locked in the cabinet
questions.explanation: The voice in the cabinet is not Jekyll's, and whoever is inside is desperately asking for a chemical.

questions.prompt: What do they find when they break down the cabinet door?
options: Hyde's body, dead from poison, wearing clothes far too big for him
questions.explanation: Hyde has killed himself; the clothes are Jekyll's, and Jekyll is nowhere to be found.

questions.prompt: What has changed in the will they find?
options: It now names Utterson as heir instead of Hyde
questions.explanation: Utterson also receives the papers that will explain everything.

questions.prompt: What does Jekyll ask Lanyon to do in his letter?
options: Take a drawer from his cabinet and hand it to a man at midnight
Lock him up in a hospital
questions.explanation: The messenger is Hyde, who comes for the chemicals in the drawer.

questions.prompt: What does Lanyon witness?
options: Hyde drinking the mixture and turning into Jekyll
questions.explanation: Seeing the transformation ruins Lanyon's health: he can't bear what he has seen.

questions.prompt: Why does Lanyon agree to watch?
options: Out of scientific curiosity, when Hyde offers to show him the secret
questions.explanation: Hyde lets him choose between leaving without knowing or seeing something that will change his science; Lanyon chooses to know.

chapters.title: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

questions.prompt: What was Jekyll trying to do with his experiment?
options: Separate the two sides of his nature: the respectable one and the one that sought hidden pleasures
questions.explanation: Jekyll felt the duality of human nature and wanted to give each side its own body.

questions.prompt: What starts happening that terrifies Jekyll?
options: He turns into Hyde without taking the potion, even in his sleep
questions.explanation: Hyde grows stronger: the dark side, once fed, starts to take over.

questions.prompt: Why can't he become Jekyll again?
options: The salt in the first batch was impure and he can't reproduce it
He decides to stay as Hyde
questions.explanation: The new supply doesn't work: the effect depended on an unknown impurity.

books.title: Frankenstein
books.author: Mary Shelley
books.synopsis: A young scientist brings to life a being made from human remains and runs away from his creation, never imagining the consequences.

questions.prompt: Who narrates the beginning of the novel?
options: Robert Walton, an explorer writing letters to his sister from the Arctic
questions.explanation: Walton rescues Victor on the ice; his ambition to discover mirrors Victor's.

questions.prompt: How does Victor react when his creature comes to life?
options: He cares for it like a son
He presents it to the university
He feels horror and disgust, and runs away, abandoning it
questions.explanation: Being abandoned by its creator is the root of the tragedy.

questions.prompt: What injustice happens after little William's death?
options: Justine, the family's servant, is convicted and executed even though she is innocent
questions.explanation: Victor knows the creature is guilty, but he stays silent and lets Justine die.

questions.prompt: How does the creature learn to speak and read?
options: By secretly watching the De Lacey family in their cottage
questions.explanation: In hiding, the creature learns language and history, and longs to be accepted by that family.

questions.prompt: What makes the creature hate humans?
options: The violent rejection he faces again and again despite his good intentions
questions.explanation: The creature says: "I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend".

questions.prompt: What does the creature demand from Victor?
options: To create a female companion as deformed as he is, to live with far from humans
questions.explanation: He asks for company so he won't be alone; Victor agrees at first.

questions.prompt: What does Victor do with the creature's companion?
options: He destroys her before finishing her, fearing they will reproduce
He finishes her and sets her free
He hands her over to Walton
questions.explanation: The creature sees this and swears: "I shall be with you on your wedding-night".

questions.prompt: How does the creature carry out his threat?
options: He kills Victor at the wedding
He kills Elizabeth on the wedding night
He burns down the family home
questions.explanation: He had already murdered Clerval; with Elizabeth gone, Victor loses everything.

questions.prompt: How does the creature react to Victor's death?
options: He mourns over the body and says he will kill himself in the far north
questions.explanation: The ending shows the creature in despair: he hated his creator, but he also needed him.

books.title: The Stranger
books.author: Albert Camus
books.synopsis: Meursault, an office clerk in Algiers, lives with an indifference that society is not willing to forgive.

questions.prompt: What stands out about Meursault's behavior at his mother's vigil?
options: He doesn't cry, and he smokes and drinks coffee with milk next to the coffin
questions.explanation: His lack of visible grief will be used against him later.

questions.prompt: How does Meursault answer when Marie asks if he wants to marry her?
options: That it doesn't matter to him, but if she wants to, they can
That he will think about it for a year
questions.explanation: Meursault doesn't fake feelings he doesn't have: to him, the question isn't important.

questions.prompt: What does Meursault say about the moment he shoots the Arab?
options: The sun, the heat and the glint of the knife daze him; he fires once and then four more times
He is defending himself from an armed attack
He does it to rob him
questions.explanation: The crime happens almost without a reason; the last four shots are "like knocking four quick times on the door of unhappiness".

questions.prompt: What does Meursault's trial focus on?
options: His indifference to his mother's death more than the crime
questions.explanation: The prosecutor accuses him of burying his mother "with crime in his heart".

questions.prompt: What does Meursault say when asked why he killed?
options: That it was because of the sun
questions.explanation: The answer makes the courtroom laugh: his honesty looks absurd to the justice system.

questions.prompt: What does Meursault discover after rejecting the chaplain?
options: He opens himself to "the gentle indifference of the world" and feels at peace
He asks the court for mercy
questions.explanation: He accepts the absurdity of existence and finds that he is happy in the face of death.

books.title: The Underdogs
books.author: Mariano Azuela
books.synopsis: Demetrio Macías, a peasant from Jalisco, takes up arms and is swept along by the whirlwind of the Mexican Revolution.

questions.prompt: Why does Demetrio Macías join the fight?
options: He gets an order from Villa
The federal troops burn his house and he has to flee with his family
questions.explanation: The federal troops' violence drives him into the mountains with a group of men.

questions.prompt: Who is Luis Cervantes?
options: A student and journalist who deserted the federal army and joins Demetrio's band
questions.explanation: He talks about revolutionary ideals, but mostly looks out for himself.

questions.prompt: What does Alberto Solís express about the Revolution?
options: Disillusionment: he admires it, but sees its ideals lost in barbarism and greed
questions.explanation: Solís says: "How beautiful the revolution is, even in its very barbarism!", shortly before he dies.

questions.prompt: What changes in Demetrio's band after the taking of Zacatecas?
options: It gives itself over to looting and violence with no clear direction
It goes back to working the land
questions.explanation: Victory brings loot, drunkenness and abuse: the fight loses its meaning.

questions.prompt: What happens to Camila?
options: La Pintada kills her out of jealousy
She goes back to her ranch
questions.explanation: Camila, brought along by Cervantes through deceit, ends up a victim of the group's violence.

questions.prompt: What does Demetrio's confusion over the split between Villa and Carranza reveal?
options: That he is a political strategist
That he fights without really understanding why or against whom
That he wants to be president
questions.explanation: Demetrio only knows he is a soldier: the Revolution carries him beyond his own reasons.

questions.prompt: Where is Luis Cervantes at the start of Part Three?
options: In El Paso, Texas, safe and enjoying his profits
questions.explanation: From the United States he writes to Venancio: the opportunist survives.

questions.prompt: What does Demetrio answer when his wife asks why he keeps fighting?
options: He throws a stone into the canyon: "Look at that stone, how it keeps going..."
That he will fight until victory
That he does it for money
questions.explanation: The image expresses a force that, once set in motion, can't stop.

questions.prompt: How does the novel end?
options: In the same canyon where it all began, Demetrio is left aiming his rifle, frozen forever
Demetrio is shot by Carranza's troops
questions.explanation: The circular ending suggests violence with no way out.

books.title: The Labyrinth of Solitude
books.author: Octavio Paz
books.synopsis: An essay on Mexican identity: its masks, its fiestas, its relationship with death and its history.

questions.prompt: Why does Paz start with the pachuco?
options: Because he represents the typical Mexican
Because he is a national hero
Because his extreme attitude makes the Mexican's solitude and identity conflict visible
Because it was a political movement
questions.explanation: The pachuco neither blends in nor claims his origins: his excess reveals a shared wound.

questions.prompt: How is adolescence linked to solitude for Paz?
options: It is a stage without conflict
It is when identity is lost
It is the moment we discover our uniqueness and, with it, our solitude
questions.explanation: Like a teenager, a people asks who it is when it finds out it is different.

questions.prompt: What does the pachuco's exaggerated clothing express?
options: A defiant statement toward a society that rejects him
A fashion from his home country
questions.explanation: His style is both provocation and defense.

questions.prompt: What does the "mask" mean for Paz?
options: The closed-off reserve the Mexican uses to protect himself and hide his inner life
questions.explanation: The Mexican closes himself off to defend himself from the outside world.

questions.prompt: Why is "rajarse" (to crack open, to back down) seen as negative?
options: It means opening up or showing weakness, seen as a disgrace
questions.explanation: The ideal of the "macho" is never to crack.

questions.prompt: What is "ninguneo"?
options: Acting as if someone didn't exist, turning them into a "ninguno", a nobody
questions.explanation: Paz describes it as a form of dissimulation that cancels out the other person.

questions.prompt: What role does the fiesta play for the Mexican, according to Paz?
options: To break his solitude and reserve for a moment, in a collective explosion
questions.explanation: At the fiesta the Mexican opens up, expresses himself and communes with others.

questions.prompt: How does Paz describe the Mexican's relationship with death?
options: He seeks it out, mocks it, caresses it and celebrates it
He fears it more than other peoples do
questions.explanation: This closeness to death also reflects a certain indifference to life.

questions.prompt: What link does Paz draw between death and life?
options: How we see death reflects how we see life
questions.explanation: "Tell me how you die and I will tell you who you are".

questions.prompt: What does "la Chingada" represent in the essay?
options: The mythical violated mother, a figure tied to La Malinche and the Conquest
questions.explanation: Paz analyzes the verb "chingar" and the violence it carries.

questions.prompt: Why does Paz speak of "sons of La Malinche"?
options: Because the Mexican rejects an origin he associates with rape and betrayal
questions.explanation: For Paz, rejecting that origin explains part of the Mexican's solitude.

questions.prompt: What is "malinchismo", according to the essay?
options: The charge against those who let themselves be seduced by what is foreign
questions.explanation: The term comes from seeing La Malinche as the one who gave herself to the conqueror.

questions.prompt: What did Catholicism offer the conquered peoples, according to Paz?
options: A place in a universal order after the fall of their gods
questions.explanation: After being orphaned by the Conquest, religion gave meaning and belonging.

questions.prompt: Which figure does Paz highlight as an expression of the colonial era?
options: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
questions.explanation: Sor Juana embodies both the richness and the limits of the colonial world.

questions.prompt: How does Paz describe the colonial order?
options: As a closed and stable order, but with no room for change
questions.explanation: A world with meaning, but frozen in place.

questions.prompt: How does Paz see the liberal Reform?
options: As a continuation of the colonial era
As a break with the Indigenous and Catholic past that left a void
questions.explanation: The Reform denied tradition in order to found the country on universal ideas.

questions.prompt: What role did positivism play under Porfirio Díaz's rule?
options: It worked as an ideological mask that justified an unequal order
questions.explanation: Positivism gave a "scientific" justification to privilege.

questions.prompt: How does Paz define the Mexican Revolution?
options: As a copy of the French Revolution
As a sudden immersion of Mexico in its own being
questions.explanation: The Revolution was a discovery of what was Mexico's own more than an ideological program.

questions.prompt: What is this chapter about?
options: The role of Mexican intellectuals after the Revolution
questions.explanation: Paz reviews how thinkers and artists tried to shape modern Mexico.

questions.prompt: Which intellectual does Paz highlight for his education project?
questions.explanation: Vasconcelos led a large education and culture campaign after the Revolution.

questions.prompt: What tension do Mexican intellectuals face, according to Paz?
options: Between the countryside and the city
Between serving the State and keeping their critical independence
questions.explanation: Many intellectuals worked with those in power and lost their critical distance.

questions.prompt: What famous statement closes the main body of the essay?
options: That Mexico should cut itself off from the world
That the Indigenous past will return
That the Revolution ended in failure
That for the first time in our history we are contemporaries of all mankind
questions.explanation: Mexico finds itself part of the problems of the modern world.

questions.prompt: What does Paz propose in the face of the modern crisis?
options: That Mexico think for itself about the problems it shares with everyone
Going back to the colonial era
questions.explanation: Mexican solitude becomes part of universal solitude.

books.title: The Prince
books.author: Niccolò Machiavelli
books.synopsis: A treatise written in Renaissance Florence on how power is won and kept, as it really is and not as it should be.

questions.prompt: To whom does Machiavelli dedicate The Prince?
questions.explanation: Machiavelli offers the book as his most valuable gift: his knowledge of statesmen.

questions.prompt: Why does Machiavelli hold up Cesare Borgia as a model?
options: Because he was a kind prince
Because he inherited a stable kingdom
Because, although he won his state through his father's fortune, he skillfully made it secure
questions.explanation: Borgia shows how virtù can hold on to what was gained by fortune.

questions.prompt: What does Machiavelli say about cruelties that are "well used"?
options: That they can never be justified
That they should be applied little by little
That they bring the prince glory
That they should be done all at once, at the start, and not repeated
questions.explanation: Discussing Agathocles: injuries should be done all at once; benefits, little by little.

questions.prompt: What does Machiavelli think of mercenary troops?
options: That they are useless and dangerous: disunited, ambitious and disloyal
That they are the best defense
That they are cheap and loyal
That they should be combined with allies
questions.explanation: He blames Italy's ruin on having relied on mercenaries.

questions.prompt: What kind of army does he recommend?
options: Auxiliary troops from a powerful ally
Your own arms, made up of subjects or citizens
questions.explanation: Without its own arms, no principality is safe.

questions.prompt: According to Chapter XIV, what should a prince devote himself to above all?
options: The art of war, even in times of peace
questions.explanation: Neglecting military preparation is the main cause of losing a state.

chapters.title: Chapters XV–XXIII: The Qualities of the Prince

questions.prompt: What method does Machiavelli propose in Chapter XV?
options: Speaking of the "effectual truth" of things, of how people live and not how they ought to live
questions.explanation: Whoever gives up what is done for what ought to be done learns his own ruin.

questions.prompt: Is it better to be loved or feared, according to Machiavelli?
options: If you can't be both, it is safer to be feared, but without being hated
It is always better to be loved
It is better to be hated than despised
questions.explanation: Fear is held in place by punishment; love depends on people's changing will.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the prince must be "a fox and a lion"?
options: He must be solitary and a hunter
He must combine the cunning to spot traps with the strength to frighten off wolves
He must be cruel to everyone
He must trust only his army
questions.explanation: The lion can't defend himself from traps and the fox can't defend himself from wolves: you need to be both.

questions.prompt: How much of our actions does fortune govern, according to Machiavelli?
options: About half; the other half is left to us
questions.explanation: He compares fortune to a flooding river that you can build dikes against in calm times.

questions.prompt: Why did the Italian princes lose their states?
options: Because of their own negligence, not bad luck
questions.explanation: Blaming fortune is the excuse of someone who didn't prepare.

questions.prompt: What does the final chapter call for?
options: For a prince to free Italy from the foreign "barbarians"
For Italy to submit to France
For the Roman Empire to be restored
For the principalities to be dissolved
questions.explanation: The exhortation ends with lines by Petrarch about virtue against fury.
